cards.title: How has the Legislative Intelligence Platform grown over time?
questions: how has the legislative intelligence platform grown over time
how did the legislative project start
how much did the bill model improve
cards.answer: It started as my early data engineering work: a legislation and higher-education trending news project where I scraped and consolidated data from Govinfo and Voteview, tested news APIs, and used fuzzy matching and topic modeling to pull legislative acts out of local news. The first platform version used two-stage LLM summarization, semantic chunking, FAISS and MiniLM vector search, and RAG to extract 12+ signals per bill, feeding a Microsoft Copilot chatbot on GPT-4.1 for executive questions. Its stage-specific passage models were around 67% accurate, with a beta dashboard on Azure App Service. The production platform I delivered in August 2026 reframed prediction as survival and runs as a multi-service Azure app rescoring 50,501 bills every day. After I rebuilt the training corpus in September, the retrained model reached 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall on a held-out General Assembly, with a median of 21 days' warning.

cards.answer: Each agent has a defined role, its own niche domain knowledge, responsibilities, history and persistent memory. A program manager, a principal architect and a founder agent coordinate the work and make decisions between the others. They hand tasks between departments, and file ownership is enforced, so an agent can only change what it owns. Decisions go into shared records, and a job queue manages schedules, dependencies, retries and approval gates. I can swap an agent's "brain" for the task: a stronger cloud model like Claude for demanding work, or one of about 20 models stored locally to save tokens. I decide when it's worth spending money. cards.answer: Breaking down the word itself: "idem" is Latin for "the same", and "potent" comes from the Latin for "power" or "ability". So idempotent means, roughly, "having the same effect": doing something again has no additional effect after the first time. In a pipeline, that means a retry can't create duplicate records or payments.

cards.title: How do you know the bill passage model isn't too good to be true?
questions: how do you know the bill passage model isn't too good to be true
how accurate is the bill passage model
how did you validate the legislative model
how do you prevent data leakage
cards.answer: A model this accurate at predicting passage should make you suspicious, because procedural history leaks the answer. So I apply the leakage guard at a single point before aggregation, split at bill level rather than row level, and keep the raw labeled history as an audit artifact so the guard can be inspected rather than trusted. That suspicion paid off. In September 2026 I traced gaps in the training corpus to a status filter: passed bills were almost missing, and resolutions were pooled with bills, inflating the success rate to 30.4% from a true 13.2%. I rebuilt the corpus from 46,815 to 117,722 bills and retrained on the corrected definitions. The honest numbers are the ones I publish now: on a held-out General Assembly, 75.1% precision and 76.2% recall at a 0.70 threshold, with a median of 21 days' warning before the floor vote. Adding each bill's title and synopsis lifted introduction-time ROC-AUC from 0.561 to 0.845, confirmed by an ablation study and three leakage checks. Catching your own inflated numbers is the job.

cards.answer: I wrote an eight-stage pipeline design and a 116-column manifest schema that every stage reads and writes. Every field has exactly one owner: no stage writes a column another stage owns. That one rule is what makes each part independently testable, re-runnable and replaceable by an engineer other than me. If a stage breaks, you can fix and re-run just that stage without wondering what else it touched.

cards.answer: It's the production build that brings three of my archival AI proofs of concept, for email, images and mixed-format legacy files, together into one operational pipeline for the University Library and AITS Information Governance. cards.title: How did you discover the archive throughput problem?
questions: how did you discover the archive throughput problem
why did you evaluate vllm
how do you find performance bottlenecks
cards.answer: Summarization was running at 34.78 seconds per record one at a time. That works out to roughly 966 hours for 100,000 records, and I traced it to the model being reloaded on every call. That led to a controlled serving-stack evaluation, which showed the real constraint was request serialization, not the hardware. Moving the backend to vLLM gave a 6.22x gain on the same hardware and cut full-corpus image processing from 22 hours to 3.7.

cards.answer: During stakeholder review I found that a column shown to leadership as a likelihood had never been calibrated against what actually happened, and readers were taking it literally. I replaced it with observed-rate bands, with cut points frozen out-of-time and validated by leave-one-year-out testing, and I wrote the stakeholder communication explaining the change. A number leadership reads as a probability has to behave like one.

cards.answer: The workforce planning system's platform was decommissioned and the developer who wrote it had left. The workflow, its SQL, the trained model and the documentation were all gone, with no recoverable backup, a quarterly deliverable due and the stakeholder blocked mid-cycle. I ordered the recovery by how perishable the evidence was rather than by what was convenient. I reconstructed the specification from surviving output files and recovered handoff notes, then restored the outstanding deliverable and verified it against three prior production runs. I also told the stakeholders, without being asked, that the model had been retrained. They needed to know.

what kind of manager do you work best with
cards.answer: I worked for about three and a half years under a manager who later became the University of Illinois System's Chief Data and Analytics Officer, and he's my model for it. He gave guidance and oversight while still giving people room to lead and grow. I always felt trusted to own my work, and I knew he was there for support, direction and advocacy when I needed it. He noticed and appreciated hard work, and he made opportunities for other people to lead. He was also brilliant at bringing people together. Working across three universities and many departments is complicated, and he could communicate, handle disagreements diplomatically and build consensus between groups with very different priorities. That balance of trust, support and connection is what I try to give my own team.

cards.answer: As the team lead I supervised data science analysts and interns, and we covered a lot of ground. On the legislative work, team members automated ingestion from LegiScan and ILGA, applied topic modeling, clustering and LLM summarization to bill text, built Tableau dashboards and network graphs of trends across states, and explored a graph-based recommender that predicted how legislators would vote by treating members as users and bills as items. Other projects included job classification standardization with TF-IDF, cosine similarity and retrieval-augmented techniques; procurement data classification over millions of rows using embeddings, clustering and zero-shot classification; screen-readable accessibility versions of Tableau files for people with disabilities; and machine learning and time-series models for student enrollment.

cards.title: What's the project you're proudest of?
questions: what's the project you're proudest of
what are you most proud of building
what's your best project
what project best shows how you think
cards.answer: The projects I'm proudest of are my two most recent personal projects, Skyrule and Agent City. Plenty of people have tried to build what each of them does, but none of them approached it the way I did. Skyrule is an AI relational-intelligence platform that helps people understand themselves and the people in their life, built by a team of AI agents I direct. Agent City is the 3D world I built to see and work with those agents: each has an office, and I can walk in and talk through its work. What makes me proud isn't the technical complexity. It's the approach: taking problems people have tried to solve for years and looking at them through a completely different lens. They're the clearest examples of how I work. I'm not interested in reproducing what's already been built; I want to find a better, more intuitive or entirely unexpected way of doing it.
